rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.subtype: Approach: safety first then triage [Thinking]
rows.description: When floodwater enters a rented flat, the person ranks needs: people and documents first, then medicines, phone and power bank, and only later furniture and electronics.

rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.subtype: Approach: following official alerts and evacuation guidance [Action]
rows.description: The person watches local authority alerts, moves family to a designated relief shelter or relatives on higher ground, and avoids risky attempts to save belongings from rising water.

rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.subtype: Approach: ignoring warnings and hoping it passes [Pitfall]
rows.description: Having seen mild floods before, the person dismisses the alert and delays leaving. Roads close overnight, and rescue becomes harder and riskier for the whole family.

rows.subtopic: Facing a natural disaster at home
rows.subtype: Approach: rebuilding in stages [Revision]
rows.description: After the disaster, the person repairs essentials first, then postpones cosmetic work, and adjusts the budget as claims arrive, adapting to money as it becomes known.

rows.subtopic: Supporting a friend in crisis
rows.subtype: Approach: noticing warning signs and taking them seriously [Thinking]
rows.description: A teen sees a friend withdraw, stop eating lunch and say things like nothing matters, and decides these changes are serious enough to act on rather than something he should just wait out.

rows.subtopic: Supporting a friend in crisis
rows.subtype: Approach: rehearsing what to say [Thinking]
rows.description: Before approaching a struggling friend, a student plans simple words such as I have noticed you seem low and I am worried about you, and what to do if the friend gets angry or shuts down.

rows.subtopic: Supporting a friend in crisis
rows.subtype: Approach: trying to fix everything alone [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student becomes his friend's only support, answers messages through the night and hides how bad it is, until his own sleep and marks collapse and the friend still has no professional help.

rows.subtopic: Supporting a friend in crisis
rows.subtype: Approach: caring for own limits and feelings [Revision]
rows.description: After several heavy conversations, a teen notices she is exhausted and anxious, talks to her mother about it, and agrees to share the support with adults, keeping a friendly role only.

rows.subtopic: Solving a puzzle
rows.subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]
rows.description: A child tries one piece after another at the same gap in a jigsaw until one fits, without thinking about the picture on it.

rows.subtopic: Solving a puzzle
rows.subtype: Approach: simple step list [Thinking]
rows.description: A child says, "Edges first, then the sky, then the house." Sorting flat-sided pieces first makes a frame to work inside.

rows.subtopic: Solving a puzzle
rows.subtype: Approach: forcing and magical thinking [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child presses a wrong piece down hard and says, "It wants to go here." Liking the idea outweighs the evidence of the shapes not matching, and the piece bends.

rows.subtopic: Solving a puzzle
rows.subtype: Approach: asking an adult [Revision]
rows.description: Stuck on the last corner, a child asks father, who shows the piece's picture and where the colour continues. The child then finds the next match unaided.

rows.subtopic: Fitting shapes into holes
rows.subtype: Approach: trial and error [Action]
rows.description: A toddler picks up a star block and pushes it against the circle hole, then the square, then the triangle, testing each hole until one finally accepts it.

rows.subtopic: Fitting shapes into holes
rows.subtype: Approach: imitation [Thinking]
rows.description: Mother drops the star into its slot, and a toddler copies the drop but holds the piece flat, sees it bounce off and starts again from the top.

rows.subtopic: Fitting shapes into holes
rows.subtype: Approach: forcing the piece [Pitfall]
rows.description: A toddler hammers a square block on the round hole with a palm again and again. The force feels like effort, but nothing about the shape of the block changes.

rows.subtopic: Fitting shapes into holes
rows.subtype: Approach: turning the piece [Revision]
rows.description: The block will not go in, so a toddler rotates it a quarter turn and tries again. The change in angle, rather than the hole, is what the toddler adjusts.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: owning up straight away [Action]
rows.description: After breaking a neighbour's window with a cricket ball, a boy goes to the door with his father, admits it and offers to help pay, and is surprised to find the neighbour is kind.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: imagining the consequences of each choice [Thinking]
rows.description: A girl who spilled ink on the sofa thinks that a lie may be found and make her parents angrier, while the truth costs a scolding now but keeps their trust.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: blaming a sibling or the dog [Pitfall]
rows.description: A child says his little sister broke the vase to escape punishment, and then feels awful watching her get scolded, and the lie needs more lies to hold it up.

rows.subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
rows.subtype: Approach: confessing late after first lying [Revision]
rows.description: After telling his mother he had finished homework, a boy feels bad through the evening, goes to her before bed and tells the truth, and she appreciates it although she still asks him to complete the work.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: pros-and-cons list with a fixed deadline [Thinking]
rows.description: An engineer unhappy in a first job writes what is gained and lost by staying versus leaving, and sets a date, three months away, to decide. A deadline prevents endless brooding.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: find out what exactly is wrong using five whys [Thinking]
rows.description: The person asks why the job feels bad, then why again, and finds that the real problem is a lack of learning and an unclear role, not the pay. Root-cause thinking changes what to ask for or look for.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: quit on the day of a bad meeting [Pitfall]
rows.description: Humiliated in a review, the employee sends a resignation email that evening with no other offer. The impulse feels like freedom, but leaves a gap in income and burned bridges.

rows.subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
rows.subtype: Approach: decide to stay with a set review and adjust [Revision]
rows.description: After the trial, the person chooses to stay for six more months with a written goal for skills and pay, and a scheduled review. If the goal is missed, the exit plan is ready.
